doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Singing with Art Tatum accompanying in Toledo
summary: Hendricks recalls Tatum accompanying him in a Toledo night club and how Tatum left the melody open, like a good arranger.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: It’s great to have the greatest exponent of a very specific style of jazz singing with us, and I hope we can see if we can understand that a little better today. You go back a ways, and I read that you used to be accompanied by Art Tatum?

For ten years in a night club in Toledo, my home town, also his home town, and I knew him all my life actually. Because I started singing at nine, professionally. I started at seven. As I say in my act, I started singing at seven, professionally at nine, before that I was a bum. I laid around the house and didn’t do nothing.
You took a few years off in your early life, okay. We can understand that.

But Art and I played all the amateur shows around Toledo. He started out on the violin, you know. His ambition was to be another Jascha Heifetz. And his mother thought to help him with his violin she’d get him a piano. And he set down to that piano and boy —
That was it. That was it.
Because we are so used to hearing him playing so much piano, that he must have been able to cut back a little bit to accompany the singing. Or how did that work?

Well what he did was he played a lot you know, but he left the melody open so that what he played surrounded you. Like a good arranger would do. Like Claus Ogerman did for Gilberto on the album called “Amaroso.” He didn’t get in Gilberto’s way but if you hear © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

those tunes without the strings, you see what he did. He just filled everything out. And that’s what I did. He knew the melody to everything. So he left that to you to sing it. And everything else he just put there.
